scope: Twenty-third expansion batch: 12 controlled exercises. Three outside-group hoka exclusions contrast with three within-group naka/uchi denials in matched key-holder, exhibition-staff and desk-book contexts. Three shared hoka/shika no-alternative answers contrast with three koto-wa-nai no-need answers using wait, redo and borrow. Shared equivalents are not independently discriminated targets.

sources.section: Exact 他/外, reading hoka: sense 4 except/other than with a negative sentence, explicitly including ...hoka-ni...nai and ...suru-hoka-nai; sense 5 addition separately covers noun-no-hoka and verb-hoka. No spelling restriction on the exclusion sense. These entries support recognition, not equal frequency or automatic naturalness of invented examples.

sources.publisher: Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten via Kotobank
sources.section: Exact ほか【外・他】 entry, noun [1]4 and particle [2]: other persons/things, and restriction with a following negative expression. The page's leading Daijisen と【外】 entry is a different reading and is not the hoka evidence.
Exact 中, reading naka, sense 2 among/within. Not the earlier chuu suffix entry, the temporal sense or the middle-quality sense.

Exact 内/中, reading uchi, sense 3 among/out of, with note as ...no-uchi and usually written in kana; no spelling restriction. The 裡/裏 spellings appear only in the separate state/condition sense and are not imported into these group-membership answers. Temporal, home and first-person uses are not the target.

Actual meaning, usage, formation and detailed grammar sections: no other available method; dictionary-form verb + hoka-nai; shika-nai can have the same meaning; hoka-nai is somewhat more formal and shika-nai more common in conversation. The optional sense of resignation is not a requirement. Alternate-form section explicitly gives hoka-wa-nai and polite hoka-arimasen. Broad claims embedded in sample life situations are not generalized.

Actual meaning and formation sections: V(dictionary) + shika-nai and V(dictionary) + (yori) hoka (shikata-ga) nai. The taxi teaching sequence explicitly removes train and bus alternatives. Its emphasis on resignation is qualified using Hedgehog's sometimes account; the emotion is not made a grading rule. The longer shikata-ga expansion is acknowledged but outside the named basic endings.

Actual About text describes no other option after verbs and explicitly allows ni, wa or ni-wa between hoka and nai. Combined with Nihongo NET's optional yori and Hedgehog's bare/wa variants, this supports the eight hoka endings. No universal emphasis ranking or claim of identical register is adopted. The supplied numeric alias in a search summary was not used.

sources.publisher: The Japan Foundation, Nihongo Kokusai Center; Yasuko Ichikawa
sources.section: Actual heading こと (1), section 3, B fixed expressions, subsection 4) ことはない: explicitly distinguishes unnecessary action from negative experience/occasion. Example 20 explains that making a special trip is unnecessary because email or telephone suffices. Only this scoped no-need claim is used, not the page's other simplified koto/no restrictions.

authoringNotes: All scenarios are original. Source recognition and formation evidence do not establish every invented sentence's naturalness; retain independent review of all literal completions and learner-facing feedback.

The six group questions explicitly request a word from hoka/naka/uchi, in kana or kanji, between printed no and ni-wa. Accept hoka/他/外 for outside exclusion and naka/中/uchi/内 for within-group denial. Naka and uchi are a shared class here, not rival correct and incorrect options. This is not an unrestricted inventory of possible group expressions.

The universe is six staff, this exhibition's staff or the books on this desk. Every outside example separately establishes that all named members qualify; every inside example separately establishes qualifying outsiders. Do not attribute those additional facts to the exclusion or membership construction alone.

The six verb questions print dictionary-form wait/redo/borrow and request one of the named basic plain kana endings: hoka-nai with optional yori and ni/wa/ni-wa, shika-nai, or koto-wa-nai. Include all nine no-alternative endings. Kanji hoka/無い, polite or past endings, shikata-ga expansions, hitsuyou-wa-nai and other paraphrases are outside that visible form task, not universally wrong Japanese.

The three no-alternative buttons display hoka-nai, shika-nai and yori-hoka-nai respectively, but all accept the same nine endings. This is three shared examples, not three independent examples for each variant. Necessity is relative to a stated goal and available routes, not proof of impossibility of every imaginable alternative or of successful completion.

No-need koto-wa-nai is supported by reassurance and satisfied requirements, with explicit optional improvement and borrowing permissions. It is not prohibition, inability or a claim that the event never happens. No-alternative hoka/shika does not require resentment or resignation.

The full linked article inventory and prior additive hoka/comparison and no-need foundation exercises were screened. This batch adds exclusion and no-alternative practice without replacing existing addition, comparison, intention, possibility or time-window exercises. Unrestricted mixed selection remains a separate plan item.

Search summaries conflated sources and supplied mismatched or unverified URLs, including books, TUFS, Maggie Sensei, numeric Bunpro aliases and other sites. They were navigation leads only; no uninspected book or page is claimed as evidence. The actual dated Nihongo NET URL and named Bunpro and Hedgehog pages above were inspected. Bunpro's separate hoka-ni-mo/hoka-ni-wa page was inspected but its broad negative-sentence restriction is not adopted.

All 293 earlier exercise records and IDs are preserved. The learner article gains only a scoped hoka subsection and two reference bullets. The contract and README describe bounded shared-answer coverage; no Android schema, UI, grading, counter or SRS behavior changes.
